116a-bits.png: Engineering mode (Gate 15.1): one byte in binary, hexadecimal and two’s complement — click a bit to flip it; Shannon’s 1948 naming of the bit; NIST’s binary prefixes.
116b-gates.png: Logic gates: XOR with live inputs and its truth table; NAND alone rebuilding NOT, AND, OR and XOR; Boole’s x² = x (1854) and Shannon’s switching-circuit analogy (1938, with his hindrance convention).
116c-adder.png: Adding with gates: 9 + 12 through a 4-bit ripple-carry adder — every carry and sum bit computed by the gates; the answer needs a fifth bit.
117a-junction.png: Semiconductors (Gate 15.2): Shockley’s 1949 p-n junction equation (4.13) as a live current–voltage curve — 12 mA at +0.6 V for I_s = 1 pA, kT/q = 25.85 mV; silicon’s 1.12 eV band gap and its 1107 nm absorption edge (TU Delft).
118a-noyce.png: Integrated circuits (Gate 15.3): Noyce’s US 2,981,877 (filed 1959) — the planar process step by step in his own words (oxide, photoengraved windows, metal leads over the oxide), a schematic section after his Fig. 2, and his original drawing sheet.
118b-kilby.png: Kilby’s US 3,138,743 (filed February 1959): the integrated circuit in one body of semiconductor, with drawing sheet 4.
119a-computer.png: The stored-program computer (Gate 15.4): a teaching machine laid out as von Neumann’s 1945 EDVAC report divides it — CA, CC, M, I, O — with orders and numbers in one marked memory; 6 × 7 = 42 by repeated addition, stepped cycle by cycle.
120a-information.png: Information and encoding (Gate 15.5): each character’s code point and UTF-8 bytes (1 to 4, colour-coded), built from the bit patterns and checked against Unicode’s own example; Shannon’s entropy of the text’s letter mix; Unicode 16.0–18.0 character totals.
121a-packet.png: Networks (Gate 15.6): a real 20-octet IPv4 header (RFC 791) with its one’s-complement checksum; each router lowers the Time to Live and recomputes the checksum until, at zero, the datagram is destroyed.
121b-handshake.png: TCP’s three-way handshake, RFC 9293 Figure 6 (unmodified), stepped line by line with the RFC’s own explanation.
121c-capacity.png: Shannon’s Theorem 17 (1948): 20 MHz at 25 dB signal-to-noise carries at most 166 Mbit/s; capacity per hertz grows only logarithmically with power.
122a-datacentres.png: Data centres (Gate 15.7): U.S. data-centre electricity from LBNL’s 2025 Update (CC BY 4.0) — 192 TWh (4.7 %) in 2024, Reference Case 464 TWh in 2028 and 649 TWh in 2030 (range 521–843); PUE as LBNL defines it, and a one-facility calculator.
